prompt.context: The city of Chicago is planning to sell the rights to all of its parking meters for 20 years to a private company. The idea is that in exchange for a lump sum, the city of Chicago would turn over the operation and revenue stream of its ~40,000 parking spaces to a private operator. The deal will bring in a big amount of cash for a cash-strapped city and relieve it of the responsibility of maintaining meters. The city is planning to use a competitive bidding process with the highest bidder winning the contract. Bidders will be expected to set the prices for their parking meters and should be aware that they bear the risk of consumer demand for parking spaces and should factor that in when pricing their bids. Additionally, the contract also requires a high-tech upgrade replacing the old coin-based meters with new machines that accept cash, credit or debit cards, which is a service enhancement that should be incorporated in the bid.
prompt.question: Your consulting firm has been hired by the Company Parking GenNext to give a reasonable price for the rights to collect all money from Chicago meters over a 20-year timeframe to win the competitive bid. Note: money collected on parking tickets goes to the city, not the company. How would you go about estimating it?

clarifying_info.q: How many parking spaces are there and how are they priced?
clarifying_info.a: There are ~40,000 metered spaces. Chicago uses a three-ring structure: Ring I (Downtown Loop) = $3/hr, 3% of meters; Ring II (Central Business District) = $2/hr, 16% of meters; Ring III (Suburbs + Others) = $1/hr, 81% of meters.

clarifying_info.q: What are the usage assumptions for each ring?
clarifying_info.a: Ring I: 12 hours/day; Ring II: 8 hours/day; Ring III: 4 hours/day. Assume weekend and weekday usage are the same. Assume 30 days/month, 12 months/year.

clarifying_info.q: What is required for the one-time meter upgrade?
clarifying_info.a: The 40,000 old single-space coin-operated meters will be replaced with 5,000 new multi-space meters (each handling 8 spaces). Unit cost per new meter is ~$20,000 including installation.

clarifying_info.q: What are the recurring operating costs?
clarifying_info.a: Assume one person needed to monitor 10 new machines (80 spaces). Average wage is $10/hr for 8 hours/day for 300 days/year. Maintenance cost is $200 per machine per month.

clarifying_info.q: Should we apply a growth rate or discount rate?
clarifying_info.a: For numerical calculations, assume zero growth rate. Time value of money can be ignored for purposes of this case.

exhibits.title: Revenue and Usage Assumptions - Number and Price of Meters
exhibits.shows: A table showing Chicago three-ring meter pricing structure with ring description, price per hour, and percentage of total meters for each ring
exhibits.data: Ring I (Downtown Loop): $3/hr, 3% of 40,000 meters = 1,200 meters; Ring II (Central Business District): $2/hr, 16% = 6,400 meters; Ring III (Suburbs + Others): $1/hr, 81% = 32,400 meters; Total: 40,000 meters

framework: Stage 1 - Valuation estimate: calculate 20-year revenue minus 20-year costs to arrive at a bid price (classic revenue/expense framework)
Revenue: estimate annual revenue per ring using (meters x hours/day x price/hr x 30 days x 12 months), then multiply by 20 years
Costs (one-time): capital expenditure to replace 40,000 old meters with 5,000 new multi-space meters at $20K each
Costs (recurring): annual labor and maintenance costs, multiplied by 20 years
Bid price = 20-yr revenue minus 20-yr total costs (represents PV of free cash flows)
Stage 2 - Creative/qualitative follow-up: alternative pricing strategies, technological opportunities, reputation and service quality
Risk factors: changes in consumer demand, population shifts, technology disruption (driverless cars, ride-sharing), preference for cycling

questions.prompt: Calculate annual revenue for each ring and total 20-year revenue (assuming zero growth).
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate annual revenue per ring as: meters x hours/day x price/hr x 30 days x 12 months. Then sum and multiply by 20. Strong candidates proactively identify the ring structure and apply correct meter counts.

math.setup: Annual revenue per ring = meters x hours/day x $/hr x 30 days x 12 months
steps: Ring I: 1,200 meters x 12 hrs x $3/hr x 30 x 12 = $15,552,000
Ring II: 6,400 meters x 8 hrs x $2/hr x 30 x 12 = $36,864,000
Ring III: 32,400 meters x 4 hrs x $1/hr x 30 x 12 = $46,656,000

questions.prompt: Calculate the one-time capital investment required to upgrade the meters.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that 40,000 old single-space meters are replaced by 5,000 new multi-space meters (8 spaces each). Total capex = 5,000 x $20,000.

math.setup: New meters = 40,000 spaces / 8 spaces per meter = 5,000 machines; Total capex = 5,000 x $20,000

questions.prompt: Calculate annual recurring costs (labor + maintenance) and total 20-year recurring costs.
questions.guidance: Candidate should estimate both staffing costs (500 workers x wage) and maintenance costs (5,000 machines x $200/month x 12). Strong candidates derive headcount from the 1-per-10-machines ratio.

math.setup: Labor: workers = 5,000 machines / 10 = 500 people; annual wage per worker = $10 x 8 hrs x 300 days. Maintenance: 5,000 machines x $200/month x 12 months.
steps: Annual wages = 500 x $10 x 8 hrs x 300 days = $12,000,000

questions.prompt: Combine revenues and costs to produce a bid price estimate.
questions.guidance: Candidate should subtract total 20-year costs from 20-year revenue to arrive at the maximum rational bid price. The casebook treats this as PV of free cash flows, ignoring time value of money per instructions.

math.setup: Bid price = 20-yr revenue minus (one-time capex + 20-yr recurring costs)

brainstorming.prompt: What other considerations should Parking GenNext think about beyond the base financial model? Consider alternative pricing strategies, technology opportunities, and public image/service quality.

categories.name: Alternative Pricing Strategies
ideas: Variable/surge pricing during peak hours or high-demand periods
Leasing or reserving specific spots to individuals or businesses on a subscription basis
Time-of-day pricing tiers to maximize revenue during rush hours

categories.name: Technology and Revenue Enhancement
ideas: Mobile app informing drivers of nearby available parking spaces
In-app payment and time-extension to reduce meter-expired situations
Real-time parking availability data sold to navigation/mapping apps as ancillary revenue
Data analytics on usage patterns to optimize pricing dynamically

categories.name: Demand Risk Factors
ideas: Population growth or decline in Chicago over 20 years
Shifting consumer preferences toward biking, walking, or public transit
Rise of ride-sharing reducing parking demand
Economic cycles affecting downtown commercial activity

categories.name: Reputation and Public Image
ideas: Strategy to demonstrate service quality improvement vs. city-run operation
Transparent pricing and clear signage to build public trust
Customer service protocols for disputes and complaints
Community engagement to manage perception of privatization

recommendation: The maximum rational bid for the 20-year rights to Chicago parking meters is approximately $1.4 billion, based on ~$2 billion in projected revenue minus ~$600 million in total costs (capex + recurring operations)
This is the breakeven bid; Parking GenNext should bid below this to ensure a positive return, adjusting downward to reflect demand risk, discount rate, and required profit margin
risks: Demand risk: usage could decline over 20 years due to ride-sharing, driverless cars, or preference shifts toward alternative transport
Revenue risk: inability to raise prices if politically sensitive or public backlash occurs
Technology risk: new parking/payment technologies may disrupt the model mid-contract
Regulatory risk: city regulations limiting pricing flexibility
next_steps: Model multiple demand scenarios (base, bear, bull) with corresponding growth rates to stress-test the bid
Assess an appropriate discount rate to convert nominal cash flows into a true present value
Explore alternative revenue streams such as advertising on machines or data licensing to improve returns
Define a service quality improvement plan to address public concerns about privatization
